title: Marketing strategy
overview: Marketing strategy coordinates objectives, research, resources and the marketing mix into a coherent plan. You must understand marketing plans, make consistent strategic choices, analyse IT/AI, and evaluate international market selection, entry methods and standardisation versus local adaptation.
syllabusPoints: Explain contents, benefits and limitations of a marketing plan.
Develop a coordinated marketing strategy consistent with objectives, target market and resources.
Analyse the changing role of IT and AI in marketing.
Analyse international marketing, market selection and entry strategies.
Evaluate pan-global standardisation versus local adaptation.

definitions.definition: A documented set of marketing objectives, research, budgets/resources, actions and controls.
The intended perception of a product/brand relative to alternatives in the target customer's mind.
Method used to enter a foreign market, e.g. exporting, licensing/franchising, joint venture or direct investment.
A largely standardised marketing approach across countries.
Changing the offer/marketing mix for local culture, law or market conditions.
Dividing a market into groups, selecting the group or groups to serve, and designing a clear relative place for the offer in their minds.
A jointly owned business formed with a partner, often combining foreign resources with local market knowledge and access.
Allowing another business to use intellectual property or produce an offer in return for fees or royalties.
Comparing actual marketing results with objectives and budgets, then taking corrective action.

sections.title: Marketing planning
content: A marketing plan states measurable objectives, the market and customer research supporting them, target segments and positioning, available finance and people, the coordinated marketing mix, actions, responsibilities, timescales, budgets and controls. It translates corporate objectives into marketing decisions and gives operations, finance and human resources a shared demand assumption.
bullets: Benefits include direction, coordination, resource allocation, risk identification, accountability and a basis for comparing actual performance with targets.
Limitations include research and preparation cost, uncertain assumptions, rigidity, internal conflict and rapid market or technology change making the plan obsolete.
A useful plan is reviewed, not ignored or followed blindly. Controls can track sales, share, contribution, acquisition cost, retention and progress against budget.

examples.label: Planning mechanism
examples.content: If an objective is 8% sales growth without entering a new market, the plan should identify which existing segments and products can deliver it, then test whether capacity, distribution and the promotional budget can support the volume.

sections.title: Coordinated strategy
content: Marketing strategy begins with segmentation, targeting and positioning (STP). The business identifies meaningfully different groups, selects those it can serve profitably, and chooses how the brand should be perceived relative to competitors. Product, price, promotion and place then need to reinforce that position and remain feasible within finance, operations and workforce resources.
bullets: Consistency with the business means the strategy fits brand, mission, competence and resources; consistency with the product means the message and channel fit its benefits and life-cycle stage; consistency with the market means it reflects target needs, rivals and external change.

Coordination traces interactions: a premium product needs quality evidence, an appropriate price, credible communication and a channel that protects service; constant deep discounting can destroy that position.
A campaign that raises demand without inventory or service capacity can increase complaints and weaken the objective it was meant to support.
The decisive mix depends on the specific objective: rapid share growth, profit, retention, repositioning or international entry may require different trade-offs.

sections.title: IT and AI
content: Information technology links websites, e-commerce, CRM, loyalty systems, social listening and marketing analytics so the business can collect data, segment customers, test messages and measure responses quickly. Artificial intelligence can predict demand, recommend products, personalise content, optimise advertising bids, support chatbots, analyse sentiment and update dynamic prices.
bullets: Potential gains include faster analysis, lower cost per contact, relevant offers, continuous experimentation and better allocation of promotion and inventory.
Bad, incomplete or historically biased data can produce confidently wrong targeting. Correlation-based predictions may fail when behaviour or the market changes.
Privacy, consent, cybersecurity, opaque decisions, discriminatory outcomes and intrusive personalisation can create legal and reputational damage.
Human review, clear objectives, representative data, access controls and comparison with a simple baseline are conditions for useful AI rather than automatic benefits.

examples.label: AI decision trade-off
examples.content: A retailer may use AI recommendations to raise conversion and average order value, but should test whether uplift exceeds software cost and whether new customers or low-data groups receive systematically poor offers.

sections.title: Selecting international markets
content: Globalisation and economic collaboration can reduce trade barriers, widen markets and enable scale, but also increase competition and expose the business to unfamiliar laws, currencies and cultures. International marketing can extend a product's life, diversify demand and use spare capacity, while adding research, coordination, logistics and adaptation cost.
bullets: Screen countries for market size and growth, income, segment fit, competition, culture, language, regulation, tariffs, political and economic risk, exchange rates, infrastructure and channel access.
Estimate accessible rather than headline demand: a large population may not have the income, distribution or legal access the offer requires.
Compare the market with business capabilities, finance and risk appetite. Reliable local research matters because secondary averages can hide regional and segment differences.
A weighted score can structure comparison, but the weights express management priorities and uncertain forecasts should not be disguised as facts.

examples.label: Market-screening interpretation
examples.content: Country A scores 8/10 for demand but 3/10 for distribution access; Country B scores 6/10 and 8/10. Choosing A solely for market size ignores whether the business can reach customers. The final judgement should weight the factors linked to the product and proposed entry mode.

sections.title: Entry modes
content: Exporting uses domestic production and has lower commitment, but transport, tariffs, agents and limited local control can weaken competitiveness. Licensing gives a local business rights to technology or a brand for royalties; franchising also transfers a business format and support. Both can expand quickly with low capital, but quality, know-how and brand control may be lost.
bullets: A joint venture shares ownership with a local partner, gaining contacts, knowledge and sometimes regulatory access, while also sharing profit, control and the risk of conflict or knowledge leakage.

Direct investment through acquisition or a new wholly owned operation gives strong control, integration and retained profit, but requires the most capital and exposes the business to political, economic and exit risk.
E-commerce can test foreign demand cheaply, but fulfilment, returns, payments, taxes, data rules and customer trust still require a local solution.
Choose by required control, speed, capital, risk, local knowledge, intellectual property, product characteristics and regulation—not by a universal ranking.

sections.title: Standardisation versus adaptation
content: A pan-global marketing strategy standardises much of the product, brand message, promotion and sometimes price or channel across countries. It can create one identity, reuse R&D and campaigns, speed launches and gain economies of scale. Local adaptation maintains local differences by changing the mix for culture, income, language, law, climate, infrastructure and competitors, increasing relevance and reducing offence or legal failure.
bullets: Standardisation can ignore different tastes, usage conditions and regulation; currency and income differences also make one price impractical.
Adaptation increases research, design, inventory, training and coordination cost and can dilute a consistent global identity.
Many businesses use global localisation: retain core brand values and product technology while adapting recipes, sizes, messages, channels or service where evidence justifies it.
Judge each element separately. A standard logo and platform can coexist with locally adapted promotion, product features and distribution.

sections.title: Data, control and strategy evaluation
content: Marketing data become useful only when connected to an objective and a decision. A dashboard should compare actual results with targets and budget, diagnose causes and trigger action. Measures can include sales by segment, market share, contribution, conversion, customer acquisition cost, retention, complaints, distribution availability and campaign response.
bullets: Triangulate internal analytics with current market research; platform clicks omit non-users and do not automatically explain motives.
Use percentage and absolute changes, suitable benchmarks and the same market definition. One short-term uplift may reflect seasonality or discounting rather than durable strategy success.
Evaluation should rank the binding condition—customer fit, finance, capacity, regulation, partner quality or data reliability—and state what evidence would change the recommendation.

examples.label: Integrated strategy check
examples.content: An international premium launch may gain reach through a local e-commerce partner, but the product promise, price, service capacity, delivery time and culturally adapted promotion must support the same positioning. High impressions do not compensate for poor fulfilment or negative contribution.

analysisChains.title: Local adaptation
steps: The marketing mix is changed for local preferences
Customer relevance and acceptance may improve
Unit costs and coordination complexity also rise
analysisChains.evaluation: Adaptation is most justified when cultural or legal differences are material; standardisation may win where global brand consistency matters more.

analysisChains.title: Coordinating a premium marketing strategy
steps: Research identifies a segment that values reliability and service
The product and support package deliver those benefits
A premium price signals positioning and funds service
Specialist promotion and selective channels provide credible evidence
Customer satisfaction, retention and contribution may rise
analysisChains.evaluation: The strategy fails if customers do not value the difference, if competitors copy it or if operations cannot deliver the promised quality and service.

analysisChains.title: Using AI for personalised promotion
steps: Customer and response data train a prediction model
Offers are targeted to customers with a higher predicted response
Wasted contacts and acquisition cost may fall
analysisChains.evaluation: Biased or stale data, privacy concerns, opaque decisions and platform cost can outweigh the gain; test incremental uplift with human oversight.

examTips: Strategy answers should show consistency between target, positioning and the mix.
International recommendations need entry mode plus why it fits finance, control and risk.
AI is only as good as its data, objective and assumptions; evaluate human oversight and stakeholder trust.
Use numerical market, budget or response data, but challenge its definition, date, comparability and cause.
A final judgement should identify the binding constraint and explain why it outweighs credible alternatives.
commonMistakes: Treating a marketing plan as only the 4Ps.
Recommending global standardisation without considering culture/regulation.
Calling social media a complete strategy without objective/target/message/budget.

quickRecall.question: What must a marketing plan contain?
quickRecall.answer: Objectives, research, target and positioning, resources and budget, a coordinated mix, actions, responsibilities, timescales and controls.

quickRecall.question: Why must a marketing mix be coordinated?
quickRecall.answer: Each element changes the meaning and feasibility of the others, so contradictions confuse positioning and waste resources.

quickRecall.question: What is the main AI marketing trade-off?
quickRecall.answer: Faster prediction and personalisation versus data quality, bias, privacy, cybersecurity, opacity and trust risks.

quickRecall.question: How does a joint venture differ from exporting?
quickRecall.answer: A joint venture shares ownership, control, profit and risk with a local partner; exporting keeps production ownership at home with lower commitment and usually less local control.

quickRecall.question: What is a pan-global marketing strategy?
quickRecall.answer: A largely standardised product, brand and campaign across countries to gain consistency and scale.

quickRecall.question: When is local adaptation most justified?
quickRecall.answer: When customer needs, culture, language, law, income, infrastructure or competition differ enough to affect demand or delivery.
